e.t: Abisoue, also rendered Avisue, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person and occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 8:4 and once in Ezra 7:5. The available information does not include the surrounding verse text, so it does not establish what role this person has in either passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name itself, with the immediate identity and significance determined by each passage’s context.

Abōmeoula is a proper name, also rendered Avomeula. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Judges 7:22. The available information establishes its spelling and role as a name, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

Agin, also called Ayin, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, although the available information does not specify which. The name appears once in the LXX, at Joshua 19:19, and is rendered “Agin” in that occurrence. Its exact referent must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone. The two forms “Agin” and “Ayin” represent the same named entity in this record.

gl: held in no esteem; stand in ill repute
d: held in no esteem; stand in ill repute

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to be held in no esteem or to stand in ill repute. It describes a person regarded as lacking honor or respect, rather than someone viewed favorably. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Isaiah 52:14, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding context. As a verb, it expresses the condition or status of being treated as disreputable or without honor.

This adverb means “inopportunely”: it describes something done or said at an unsuitable or badly timed moment. It tells how an action occurs, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 32:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is clear: the action comes when the time is unfavorable or inappropriate.

This adjective describes someone or something as “licentious” or “intemperate”—without proper restraint and inclined toward excess. It characterizes a person or thing rather than naming an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs three times, all in Proverbs. Its central idea is a lack of self-control expressed in morally undisciplined or excessive conduct. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls more on immoral freedom or on uncontrolled excess.

This adjective means “top” or “tip”: it points to the uppermost end or point of something. It can refer to a physical extremity, so the word identifies position rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 70 times, showing that this is a recurring word for an upper end or point. Its exact sense in a particular passage depends on what object or place it describes.

This Greek LXX verb means to “stay estranged”—to remain separated or distant from someone rather than return to friendly association. It describes an ongoing condition of alienation, not merely a brief disagreement. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus: once in Genesis and three times in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and relationship being described.

e.h: Immortal and Not Subject to Death
e.t: This adjective means “immortal”: not subject to death or passing away. It describes something possessing a life or quality that does not perish. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Wisdom 19:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise reference in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its central meaning remains the enduring quality of being immortal.

Ammach is a proper name, rendered as “Ammach” or “Ammakh,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 27:2. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide an added meaning or etymological explanation. Its precise referent and role are determined by the surrounding passage, not by the name alone.

This Greek verb means “communicate”—to share information or make something known to another person. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:20. The reference identifies its only occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what was communicated and how the action functions in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “renew one's youth”: to become young or youthful again. It describes an action rather than a person, name, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 7:13. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise force in that sentence cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning is the restoration or renewal of youth. [p03:word:lxx:L701009:identity] [p01:word:lxx:L701009:reference:0]

This verb means “wake up” or “rouse”—to awaken someone or cause someone to become awake. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 49:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely who is awakened or what situation the verb describes; the word itself expresses awakening or stirring someone to wakefulness.

This adjective means “above” or “upper,” describing something located higher than another thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for position or elevation, whether referring to an upper place or something situated above. The word occurs five times in four verses, including passages in Leviticus, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what object, place, or level it describes there.

This Greek LXX verb means “give up” or “despair.” It describes abandoning hope or ceasing to expect a favorable outcome. As a verb, it expresses an action or state of losing confidence rather than merely naming sadness. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, in Deuteronomy 33:9 and 2 Maccabees 9:22. The surrounding verse determines what a person is despairing of or giving up.

This adjective describes someone or something that is doing nothing or proving ineffectual. It can refer to a lack of useful action or to an effort that accomplishes no effective result. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains inactivity or lack of effectiveness rather than successful action.

This adjective describes someone or something treated as without honour, respect, or esteem—“unhonoured; despised.” It points to a lowly or rejected standing rather than something valued or held in regard. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 7:9 and 3 Maccabees 3:23. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes being disregarded, devalued, or treated with contempt in that particular setting.

This LXX adverb means “right here,” pointing to a specific place that is present or being indicated. It directs attention to location rather than naming a person, object, or action. The word occurs 8,103 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. Its repeated use across these writings shows a common location-pointing function in Greek Scripture.

This noun means “speechlessness”: the condition of being unable or unwilling to speak. It names the absence of spoken expression rather than an action or spoken message. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 14:17. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context, but its central meaning remains the loss or absence of speech.

Achiezer is a personal name, rendered as “Achiezer” or “Akhiezer.” It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. The name occurs seven times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing six times in Numbers and once in 1 Chronicles. Without additional explanation attached to the name itself, its ordinary meaning is simply the personal designation Achiezer.

Achimelech is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as the personal name “Achimelech,” also rendered “Akhimelekh.” The name occurs seven times across seven verses, in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is identifying the individual who bears it; the particular person and role intended in any verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Baalberith is a proper name, also rendered “Vaalverith.” It identifies a named figure rather than describing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Judges 9:4. The name itself does not provide enough information here to explain the figure’s character or role; those details depend on the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning is therefore best retained as the proper name “Baalberith.”

This Greek LXX noun means “torment”—severe suffering, distress, or painful affliction. It names the painful condition a person may endure, rather than describing an action or person. The word occurs 61 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, with especially frequent use in 4 Maccabees. Its core sense remains focused on intense suffering, while the surrounding passage determines whether the torment is physical, emotional, or connected with hardship. The English rendering “torment” also appears in several translated occurrences.

This Greek LXX noun means “clod,” referring to a compact lump of earth or soil. It names a physical piece of ground rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including Job, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a clod or lump of earth.

This Greek LXX noun means “married woman” or “wife.” It identifies a woman in relation to marriage, rather than describing a woman generally. The word appears once in the LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:11. Its basic sense is therefore specific and straightforward: a woman who is married, or a wife within a marriage relationship. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how that sense functions in that particular passage.

The word is a proper name identifying a Gedōrite, also given in the lexical definition as Yethoriti. It functions as a designation rather than a general description, naming someone according to that identity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 27:28. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference there cannot be explained further, but its basic sense is the name or designation Gedōrite.

Dessa or Thessa is a proper name used as a personal or place designation in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself does not carry an ordinary descriptive meaning beyond identifying what is named. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Numbers 33, showing that it is a rare name rather than a commonly used word or action. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and the person or location being named there.

This Greek LXX verb means to turn away from something or someone. It describes a change of direction or withdrawal rather than remaining oriented toward the object in view. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges, Esther, Job, and Daniel. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the specific object or reason for turning away must be determined from each passage’s context.

This noun refers to assaying or assessing something—examining it to determine its value or standing. It describes the act or process of testing rather than the person who performs the test. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Psalms and once in Proverbs. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “hide,” referring to the outer covering of an animal. It is a noun, so it names a physical material rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning is hide.

This Greek LXX verb means “subject; subjugate”: to bring someone or something under another’s authority or control. It describes an act of placing under rule rather than merely influencing or guiding. The word appears six times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Genesis, Proverbs, Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on who is exercising authority and who or what is being brought under it.

This verb means “graft”: to join or insert one living part into another so that they grow together. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:11. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific image or point being made there.

This Greek LXX verb means “receive from”: it describes taking or accepting something that comes from another person or source. It is an action word, so it focuses on the act of receiving rather than merely possessing something. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains receiving something from a source.

This adjective means “free”: not held in bondage or under another person’s control. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes a person’s condition as free, especially in laws concerning servants and their release. It is also used more broadly for one who is not enslaved or constrained. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Emerōn is a proper personal name, preserved as “Emerōn” or “Emeron.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 1:41. The available information establishes its identity as a name, but does not provide an English meaning or enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person named.

This noun means a notion or concept—a thought or idea held in the mind. It refers to something understood or considered mentally rather than to a physical object or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 21:11. The reference identifies its location, but the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage. Its basic sense remains an idea or mental conception.

This word means “outside,” describing a position beyond an interior place or boundary. It can function as an adverb, indicating where something is, or as a preposition, relating a person or thing to what lies beyond. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 101 times, showing that it is a normal word for expressing location or separation from what is inside. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This noun means “begging”: asking others for help, especially by requesting money or support. It describes the act or practice of making such requests rather than the person who begs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach 40, showing a focused use of the term in that book. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the act of begging or appealing for needed assistance.

Esdri is a personal name in the Greek Septuagint. The lexical entry gives the name as “Esdri” and also “Ezthri,” representing two supplied spellings of the same named entity. It functions as a proper name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in two passages in Judges and one in 1 Chronicles.

Esthemōē, also represented as Esthemi, is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:19. The available information identifies the name and its spelling variants but does not provide a further lexical definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role there. Its precise significance therefore comes from the passage in which the name occurs.

This Greek LXX adverb means “immediately”: something happens at once or without delay. It describes the timing of an action, showing that it follows promptly rather than after a long interval. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its basic force remains focused on speed and direct succession, while the surrounding verse determines what action takes place immediately.

This Greek LXX adverb means “skilfully,” describing an action carried out with ability and competence. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or thing. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 13:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is clear: an action performed skilfully.

“Ephrathites” is a proper name used to identify an Ephrathite, a person designated by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Judges 12:5. Because it functions as a personal or group designation rather than a description of an action or quality, its basic meaning is simply the identity of an Ephrathite. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific person or situation involved there.

Echozob, also rendered Ekhozov, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, in Joshua 19:29. The available wording identifies the name itself, but does not provide enough information here to explain its referent or add a broader meaning. Thus, the safest plain-language understanding is that this word functions as a specific name rather than as a general description or action.

This noun means “art of painting,” referring to the practice or skill of creating pictures with paint. It names an artistic activity rather than a person or an individual painting. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 38:27. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the craft of painting.

This Greek LXX verb means “boil” or “seethe,” describing something heated until it reaches an active, bubbling state. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, at 1 Samuel 2:13. As a verb, it expresses an action or process rather than naming an object. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is becoming intensely hot and agitated.

Thapheth is a proper name, also rendered “Thafeth.” It functions as a specific identifying name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Joshua 17:8. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain the surrounding verse or identify the named referent beyond its use as a proper name there.

Thōa is a proper name, rendered “Thoa.” As a name, it functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles 18:9–10. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity, but without the surrounding verse text, it does not support a fuller description of its role there.

This word denotes the number “13.” It is an indeclinable number-word, so its basic function is to identify a quantity rather than describe an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears once, at Psalm 118:97. The available lexical wording also includes “mem,” but without surrounding verse text its precise significance here cannot be stated. Its ordinary meaning remains the number thirteen.

e.h: So That or In Order That
e.t: This word means “so; that” and usually joins one statement to another by expressing the purpose or intended result of an action. In ordinary reading, it can answer the question “for what purpose?” or show what something is meant to bring about. It functions as a conjunction, helping connect an action with its goal rather than naming a person, thing, or quality. In the LXX, it occurs 553 times, so this is a broadly used way of expressing purpose or result.

The word refers to the hip-joint, the part of the body where the upper leg joins the pelvis. It is a noun naming this specific bodily area, not a general term for the whole leg or body. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 10:4. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular use there.

Iōsia, also written Iosia, is a personal name used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs 25 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing most often in Jeremiah and also in Kings, Chronicles, and Baruch. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as “Kaibaiseleēl” or “Keveselil.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:21. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely, but its lexical function is clear: it is a particular name preserved in the biblical place-name or personal-name record.

This adjective means “bent” or “crooked,” describing something that is not straight. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, in Proverbs 2:15. As an adjective, it identifies a quality or condition rather than an action or person. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic idea is physical or figurative lack of straightness. The word’s meaning is therefore centered on deviation from a straight path or line.

This Greek LXX verb means “stretch”—to extend something outward or draw it taut. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so the surrounding sentence shows what is being stretched and how. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus represented here, including three occurrences in Leviticus and two in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This noun means a “stinger” or “spur”—a pointed object used to prick, prod, or urge movement. It names a physical implement rather than an action or quality. In this LXX corpus, it occurs five times across Proverbs, Hosea, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a sharp point that presses or pricks.

This LXX Greek noun means “stirring.” It describes movement or something being set in motion rather than remaining still. Depending on the surrounding words, it may refer to physical movement or a disturbance, but its central idea remains activity and motion. In this Greek corpus, the word occurs nine times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any passage comes from the surrounding sentence.

This LXX adjective means “hold” and describes a space or part that contains something. Its central idea is an interior place or compartment rather than an action of grasping. The word occurs five times in the LXX corpus, across three Old Testament verses and two Deuterocanonical verses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its normal sense points to something connected with a hold or containing space.

This Greek LXX verb means “peck at”: to strike or pick at something with a beak. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality, so its precise force depends on what is being pecked and the surrounding sentence. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, including Exodus, 1 Kings, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains a repeated or pointed picking motion directed at something.

This LXX Greek noun means “noise” or “din”: a loud, noticeable sound or commotion. It names the sound itself rather than describing an action, person, or object. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Esther and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on an audible disturbance, while the surrounding verse determines what produces the sound and why it matters in that passage.

Lemona is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name used to identify a location. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:20 and Numbers 33:21. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the location’s identity but does not provide additional meaning about its history or significance.

Magdōn is a proper name identifying a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The lexical information also gives Magthon as a related form, but it does not specify whether the name refers to a person, place, or other thing. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs only once, at 1 Samuel 14:2. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly whom or what the name designates.

Makedōn or Makethon is a proper name, referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament and related historical books. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation preserved in the text. This name occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Esther, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name’s specific role in each occurrence must be understood from its immediate context.

Melcham is a proper name, also rendered Melkham. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:9. The available information establishes the name’s identity and spelling forms, but does not provide an additional lexical definition or explain the person’s role. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding genealogical context.

This proper noun means “Mēdos; Mithos,” functioning as a personal or national name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Isaiah and twice in Daniel. Its use identifies the named designation in each passage, while the surrounding verse determines its precise reference there. The word is therefore best understood as a proper name, not as a general term with several ordinary meanings.

This adjective describes someone or something “suffering hardship; in sore distress.” It points to a condition marked by difficulty, trouble, or painful circumstances rather than comfort or ease. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a description of distress or hardship.

Nadabath, also rendered Nathavath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs once in the Greek text, in 1 Maccabees 9:37. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, the identity and significance of the person must be understood from that passage itself; the name’s basic meaning is simply the person it designates.

Noo is a proper name, given as “Noo.” It is not presented as a general action, quality, or object-word, but as a specific designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:30. Since the verse text and surrounding context are unavailable, the supplied material does not establish whether Noo names a person, location, or another specific referent in that passage. Its basic lexical meaning is therefore the name “Noo.”

This LXX word means “kind that; what.” It is used as an adjective or pronoun to ask about, identify, or describe the kind or nature of something. In English Bible renderings, it commonly appears as “what,” but its fuller sense can point to the character or type of a person or thing. It occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Genesis, Job, Daniel, and other books.

This verb means to take bird omens or divine—seeking knowledge or guidance through signs, especially the behavior or flight of birds. It describes a practice rather than ordinary observation. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs eight times, in eight verses, and is used across Genesis, Leviticus, Kings, and Chronicles. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the practice of divination through omens.

This Greek LXX verb means “make even”: it describes the action of causing something to become even or level. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus, appearing twice in Isaiah and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being made even there.

This word means “not even” or “neither.” It is a conjunction or particle that adds a further negative point, joining words or statements that are also excluded. Depending on the sentence, it can deny an additional possibility or connect two negative alternatives. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 557 times, so it is a common way of expressing joined or intensified negation rather than a term naming a person, object, or action. Its exact force in any verse comes from the words and statements it connects.

This verb means “celebrate”: to take part in or express celebration. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 66:10, so its normal meaning is clear even though its broader range of use cannot be assessed from this corpus alone. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific occasion or force of the celebration there.

This adjective means “all-nourishing”: it describes something characterized as nourishing all. The word presents nourishment as broad and comprehensive rather than limited to one person or thing. Because it is an adjective, it modifies a person, thing, or reality by identifying it as all-nourishing. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 16:25. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not included here.

This verb means to bend or turn something from a straight position. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek of the Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 47:19. The available wording establishes its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would determine exactly what is being bent and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX verb means to “afford” something or to “cause” something to happen. It describes an action that brings about an effect or makes something available. The word appears 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. The precise force in any verse depends on what the verb acts upon and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains producing or supplying a result.

This verb means “pirate,” expressing an action associated with piracy. It names an action rather than a person, title, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 49:19, so it is rare within this corpus. The lexical meaning identifies the basic action, while the surrounding wording of that verse would be needed to explain the precise force of the action in context.

This verb means “plait”: to interweave or braid strands together. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Isaiah, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word presents something being formed by combining strands into an arranged, connected whole.

This adjective means “rich,” describing a person or thing possessing abundant material wealth. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, where it can identify those who have substantial possessions or resources. The word occurs 50 times in this LXX corpus, so it describes a recurring social and economic condition rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is being described.

Gentleness describes a calm, considerate quality in a person’s character and conduct. It is the opposite of harshness, pride, or rough treatment, expressing strength or authority without needless severity. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, this noun appears nine times, including passages in Esther, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise expression can vary with the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a gracious, restrained way of treating others and carrying oneself.

This verb means “demand besides”: to ask for something additional beyond an earlier demand or request. It functions as an action word, focusing on the act of requiring more rather than simply making an initial request. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:10. The reference identifies its location, while the word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “make to grow to”: it describes causing something to grow toward or become attached to a destination or point. Its basic sense focuses on the act of bringing growth into connection with something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 7:20. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is growing and what it is growing to in that passage.

This verb means “assign to.” It expresses the action of placing something under the responsibility, role, or destination given to another. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:2. This noun means “corpse,” referring to a dead human body. It is a direct, physical term for a body after life has ended, rather than a description of death as an event or of grief as an emotion. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 19 times, with repeated use in Job and Isaiah. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a dead body.

Its recorded meaning is “Reērōth; Rhiroth,” which functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or quality. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish further details about the place, its history, or its significance.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Garlic
e.t: This word means “garlic,” the pungent bulb used as food and seasoning. It is a noun naming the plant or its edible bulb. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:5, within Israel’s remembrance of foods associated with Egypt. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while the precise force of the reference must be understood from that passage. This is a Greek LXX word and should be kept distinct from Greek New Testament lexical entities.

This Greek LXX adjective means “gloomy.” It describes a person or appearance marked by sadness, heaviness, or a darkened mood. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in Genesis 40:7 and once in Sirach 25:23. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a gloomy or downcast condition.

The word means “convolvulus,” functioning as a noun—the name of a particular plant. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs twice, once in Jeremiah 26:14 and once in Nahum 1:10. e.h: Campaign or Serve as a Soldier
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “campaign” or “soldier,” describing military service or taking part in a campaign. It portrays a person acting as a soldier rather than merely referring to a military object or place. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing use across both parts of that corpus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being described.

This verb means to consent to something—to agree to it or give one’s approval. It describes an act of willing agreement rather than merely hearing, noticing, or being present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word presents consent as an intentional response: a person accepts or agrees with what is being proposed. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “pierce through at once,” describing a swift action in which something is pierced completely or in one movement. It expresses the act itself rather than a person, object, or general condition. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:26. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what was pierced and how the action functions in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “alliance”: a joining or agreement between people or groups who stand together. It refers to a united association rather than to an individual person or action. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Genesis and twice in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a formed alliance or united partnership.

This Greek LXX word means “both” and “and,” joining two words, phrases, or ideas so they are understood together. It functions as a conjunction or particle, often adding a second item while emphasizing that the first and second belong together. The word appears 245 times in the Greek LXX, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the words and clauses it connects.

“For a despotic ruler” describes something associated with a ruler who exercises oppressive or absolute authority; it can also mean “royal.” As an adjective, the word characterizes a person, possession, authority, or matter connected with such rulership rather than naming the ruler itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 3 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “quarrel”: a conflict or contentious disagreement between people. It names the dispute itself rather than describing a person’s action. The word appears three times in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical books, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on interpersonal contention, while the surrounding passage determines what caused the quarrel and how serious it was.

Chabratha is a proper name, also rendered Khavratha. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Genesis: Genesis 35:16 and Genesis 48:7. The available wording establishes the name itself, but does not provide enough context here to explain the person or place it identifies.
